## Understanding the problem
Count k in [0, n] whose binary form (no leading zeros) is a palindrome; '0' counts. For n = 9: 0,1,3,5,7,9 → 6.

A binary palindrome of length L ≥ 2 is determined by its first ⌈L/2⌉ bits (top bit forced to 1), giving 2^(⌈L/2⌉−1) palindromes per length. So count all palindromes shorter than n's bit-length in closed form, then count same-length palindromes ≤ n by comparing n against the palindrome built from n's own first half.
k: Per length L ≥ 2 there are exactly 2^(⌈L/2⌉−1) binary palindromes (top bit fixed at 1).
Palindromes shorter than n's length are counted in closed form; same-length ones are counted by ranking the first half.
Mirror the top ⌈L/2⌉ bits of n to get the smallest same-length palindrome with that prefix; compare with n.

a.n: Approach 1: Closed-form counting by bit length
a.i: Add 1 for zero. For each length l < L add 2^(⌈l/2⌉−1). For length L, take pref = n >> (L − h) with h = ⌈L/2⌉; all halves strictly between 2^(h−1) and pref yield palindromes < n, contributing pref − 2^(h−1); finally mirror pref into a full palindrome and add 1 if it is ≤ n.
s: Mirror pref (even/odd length rules) and compare to n for the final +1.
a.t: O(log n) — one pass over bit lengths plus O(log n) mirroring work.
a.sp: O(1) (O(log n) for the bit string in Python/JS).

w: This constructive counting is the only viable approach at n = 10¹⁵ (checking each integer is hopeless). Pitfalls: odd-length mirroring must exclude the middle bit from the mirrored part, remembering 0 and 1 are palindromes, and 64-bit/BigInt care in JS. Follow-up: k-th smallest binary palindrome, or palindromes in base b.
